You asked to see the wording, so the AFTER picture is the wording.

First, what the arrow actually does — I read the code rather than guessing, because it decides how the message should read. Outdenting moves the item up one level and takes everything inside it along. Nothing is deleted, and the → arrow puts it back. So the dialog must not look like a danger warning — a red "are you sure?" for a reversible move trains you to click through every dialog, including the ones that matter.

What the wording does:
• asks a plain question in the title — "Move this out to its own branch?"
• names the item and its parent, so you know which row you hit
• shows the move as now → after, rather than describing it
• says what travels with it — anything inside moves too
• says it is reversible, naming the → that undoes it
• the confirm button says Move it out, not "OK" — the button names the action, so it reads correctly if you skim.

The cause, in one line of the app’s own code:
var today = (window.selectedDate || todayISO());  // the TREE DATE, not the clock
var realToday = todayISO();  // computed right here, and NOT used for this
var isFuture = !!(date && date > today);
"Future" is measured against the date at the top of the tree. Step that date forward and yesterday’s future becomes today’s present, so the rows unhide — while the switch you actually set sits there doing nothing. realToday is already sitting on the line above, used only for "overdue".

I FIXED THIS THE WRONG WAY FIRST — corrected 2026-10-30
I measured "future" from the real clock. That stopped the leak and broke something you rely on: an item never became due no matter how far forward you read. You found it in one move.
Measured on three items due in 1, 6 and 20 days, tree date moved to +6:
ruledue in 1due in 6due in 20
tree date (original, and now)shownshownhidden ✓
clock (my first fix)hiddenhiddenhidden
The rule, as you describe it: moving the tree date forward is reading that day. Anything due by then is present and must appear; only what is still beyond it is "future". That line is back as it was.

So what was actually broken? Not this rule — the gear switch, which is the rest of this card. It could not be turned on, so there was never a way to deliberately look further ahead than the day you were reading. That half of the fix stands and is in the demo.

AND A SECOND FAULT, found because you asked for the "setting ON" picture
I could not take that picture — the switch will not turn on at all. I pressed it, read the setting back, and it was still off.
I trapped every write to the setting and watched who moved it:
hideFuture → false  by toggleHideFuture — your press
hideFuture → true  by settings() — immediately after
hideFuture → true  by settings() — and again on every render
A helper that runs on every render carries the line s.hideFuture = true; — not as a default, but as an order. So the switch flips for a fraction of a second and is overwritten before anything is drawn. It has never been able to stay on.

Proven: I changed that one line to set a default instead of forcing a value (if (typeof s.hideFuture !== 'boolean')) and the switch worked at once — setting went off, two future rows appeared, and it survived a redraw.

So card 2 is two faults in one place: the tree date leaks future items in when the switch is off, and the switch cannot be turned on to ask for them deliberately. Fixing only the first would leave you with no way to see ahead at all.

I think that is right: "what have I missed" follows the day you are reading, while "do not show me things that have not happened yet" should follow real time, or the switch means nothing. But they are two rules pulling in opposite directions, and you should be the one to say so.

You were right to ask for the ON picture. I had drawn this card without it, and it would have shipped a fix to one fault while the switch stayed dead — you would have pressed it, seen nothing, and been back here. The missing picture was the missing test.

A THIRD FAULT, found while building this
Before publishing I pressed the real gear menu item instead of calling the function my own check had been calling. It did nothing.
There are two separate switches behind one control. The gear item calls __futToggle, which writes its own flag and draws the tick and the count. But the rows are hidden by a different mechanism that watches __revealAhead, owned by a different function. So the button flipped a flag nothing was watching — and the menu was even showing the count "1" for a branch it then refused to reveal.

The third fix: the button keeps its own state, and now carries the other along with it, so one press means one thing.

What this would have cost you: shipping the first two fixes alone would have stopped the leak and left you with no way to see ahead at all — the switch would still have been dead. My check had been calling the function, so it would have passed. A check that calls the function tests the function; only pressing the button tests the button. It now presses the button.

THE RULES OF THIS BOARD — permanent, they never come off

  1. The AFTER shows the SCENARIO you raised, not a tidy example. Added 2026-10-11 in your words: "you need to show me the after picture from those scenarios, always, that is a rule you must adhere by." If you report a control at the bottom of a window, the pictures are OF a control at the bottom of that window — the BEFORE photographed in that exact state, the AFTER showing that same state fixed. A picture of the easy case proves nothing about the case you hit.
  2. EVERY change is drawn here and waits for your word — including a fix to a fix. Restated 2026-10-11 in your words: "from now on, show me on the PNG file before you do anything, then wait for my approval to put it in the demo." I had been treating a correction to something already approved as a continuation of that approval, and putting it straight on the demo. It is not. A new change is a new card, drawn, waiting, however small and however obviously right it looks to me.
  3. Minimax advises; I write the code. Changed 2026-10-11 on your instruction — "change the rules from Minimax from executioner of code to just co-brain only, I feel like a lot of the code stuff you are doing is going back and forth." Every change used to become a written brief, a round-trip and a verification step; on a one-line fix that was four steps, and its own verification was wrong three times in a row. It still advises on every turn — that part earns its place. The gate that enforced the old way is switched off, and kept so it can be switched back.
  4. When you ask to SEE it, you get a photograph of it working — not a drawing, and not the same drawing twice. A drawing is only ever a first look at something not built yet. The moment you ask again, I build it, test it and photograph the real thing. Added 2026-10-10, after I left two drawings on this board across three replies and you had to ask three times.
  5. I do not hand anything back half done. If a card says fixed, it is built, measured, gate-tested and photographed before you read the word. Added 2026-10-10, in your words: "your response must be complete and done before saying done".
  6. I find the pattern before I invent one. Before changing how anything looks, I find the control in the planner that already does that job and copy it. Added 2026-10-10, after I drew a new calendar when the app already had one, and after I changed a css rule that three controls share instead of the one you asked about. Both came from acting on what I expected instead of measuring what is there. When you ask "is that Claude or Minimax" — it is me. Minimax writes only the exact text I dictate.
  7. Your list goes up here first. Every item you raise becomes a card with a BEFORE picture, an AFTER picture and how I would fix it. Nothing is written into the planner before that.
  8. No code before you approve the card. You approve card by card. Only when you say “make it live” do I write anything.
  9. Approved is not live. A card you approve stays here as APPROVED until the build ships, so you can see what is queued.
  10. A card never leaves until you say remove. This board is the record of what you asked for, not a list of what I finished.
  11. Your words are kept, all of them — one line per thing you said. Your first quote stays at the top of the card forever; every later correction is its own dated line underneath, never merged into a paragraph, so you can check each one off. I never replace what you said with my summary.
  12. The AFTER is not one picture — it explains the new setup, step by step, in different pictures. What happens first, what happens next, what it looks like when it works. Never the same picture twice. If nothing is built yet, the card says so in plain words instead of pretending.
  13. Every question sits inside the problem it belongs to — never collected somewhere else. You read one card and answer it there.
  14. I raise what you have not thought of. Every card carries an I also thought of note: the thing your request does not decide — the crowded case, the phone, what happens to what you already have.
  15. I test it in Safari myself — before I call it done, and again after it goes live.
  16. Pictures, not paragraphs. Short words around the picture, never an essay above it.
  17. Every picture is half a page — including the step pictures. The BEFORE and AFTER are half each, and a step picture is the same size, not a thumbnail, because you have to see what is inside it. A shot of the whole browser takes the full width on its own row.
  18. EVERY APPROVED CARD IS SHOWN CONSOLIDATED — folded shut. The moment you approve one it collapses to a single line, so the board only ever shows you what still needs you. Press open beside its number to look at it again. This one is never skipped.
